title: Neural Networks With Dense Weights Are Not Universal Approximators
claim: A structured sparse kernel-signal pair, with block structure linking consecutive layers, encodes a network as a message-passing computation.
layout: 2 panels, left matrix and right column vector, labeled axes
description: The left panel is a large square grid-matrix in black and white with grayscale cells. Its rows are labeled y (source) and its columns x (target). Both axes are divided into bias and layer blocks ℓ0 to ℓ3. Most of the matrix is plain white-and-black gridlines, which means zero entries. Gray nonzero blocks sit along the diagonal, linking consecutive layers, and a dark band runs along the bottom bias row. The bottom band has vertical stripes, which show constancy over coarse intervals. The right panel is a thin vertical column of gray-scale cells labeled x (input). It is the signal, and it has the same coarse-interval structure. A wide white gap separates the panels. The eye goes first to the matrix and its diagonal gray blocks.
caption: A computational kernel-signal with 𝑑= 8. The kernel 𝐾is nonzero only on blocks linking consecutive layers and bias-to-layer blocks; visible stripes in the first/last layer blocks reflect constancy over input/output coarse intervals. The signal 𝑓 shares the same coarse-interval structure.
abstract: We investigate the approximation capabilities of dense neural networks. While universal approximation theorems establish that sufficiently large architectures can approximate arbitrary continuous functions when there are no restrictions on the weights, we show that dense neural networks do not possess this universality. Our argument is based on a model compression approach, combining the weak regularity lemma with an interpretation of feedforward networks as message passing graph neural networks. We consider ReLU neural networks subject to natural constraints on weights and input and output dimensions, which model a notion of dense connectivity. Within this setting, we demonstrate the existence of Lipschitz continuous functions that cannot be approximated by such networks. This highlights intrinsic limitations of neural networks with dense layers and motivates the use of sparse connectivity as a necessary ingredient for achieving true universality.
